Start with what emotional intelligence really is, according to the researchers who named it. You will learn to put precise names to your feelings, see how a feeling turns into an action, and map the people, places and situations that set you off.

**Emotional intelligence** (often shortened to EI or EQ) is the ability to notice emotions in yourself and others, understand what they are telling you, and use that information to guide what you think, say and do. It is not about being soft, and it is not about never getting angry. It is about handling feelings well, so that they help you instead of controlling you.

Emotional intelligence begins with pausing long enough to notice what you are feeling.
Where the idea comes from

The term was set out in a scientific paper in 1990 by two psychologists, **Peter Salovey** (Yale University) and **John Mayer** (University of New Hampshire). In 1995 the journalist and psychologist **Daniel Goleman** wrote the best-selling book *Emotional Intelligence*, which made the idea famous around the world. You will see both models in this course, because they help in different ways.

Self-awareness is the foundation; the other areas build on knowing yourself.
**Self-awareness:** knowing what you feel and why, and how it affects others.
**Self-regulation:** controlling sudden impulses and thinking before acting.
**Motivation:** working towards goals for reasons that matter to you, and keeping going after setbacks.
**Empathy:** understanding other people's feelings and points of view.
**Social skills:** building relationships, handling conflict and working well in groups.
Three myths to drop
**Myth: emotionally intelligent people are always calm and smiling.** Truth: they still feel anger, fear and sadness. They simply notice these feelings earlier and choose what to do with them.
**Myth: you are born with it or you are not.** Truth: these are skills. Like learning to drive or to sew, they improve with practice.
**Myth: emotional intelligence means pleasing everyone.** Truth: it includes saying no clearly and setting boundaries without shouting or sulking.
Worked example: the same morning, two ways

For example, Ngozi runs a small provisions shop in Onitsha and has three children. One school morning the generator will not start, the children are late, and a supplier calls to say her goods will come two days late.
Without EI: she shouts at her eldest son for being slow, snaps at the supplier, and spends the morning upset and short with customers.
With EI, step 1 (perceive): she notices her jaw is tight and her voice is rising.
Step 2 (understand): she tells herself, 'I am stressed because three things went wrong at once, not because my son is bad.'
Step 3 (manage): she takes three slow breaths, asks her son to help his sisters, and tells the supplier calmly that she needs a firm new date by 12 noon.
Step 4 (use): she uses the push of urgency to call a second supplier as a backup.
The problems are the same, but with EI she protects her relationship with her son and her supplier, and she has a backup plan by midday.
This course is not therapy

Emotional intelligence skills help with everyday stress and relationships. They do not replace a doctor, counsellor or psychiatrist. If low mood, worry or anger is lasting for weeks, affecting sleep, eating or work, or you have thoughts of harming yourself or others, please speak to a health professional, a trusted faith leader or the nearest hospital.
In the rest of this module you will practise the first ability, **perceiving and naming emotions**, because every other skill depends on it.
What EI looks like in a Nigerian home and workplace
At home: noticing that a teenager's rudeness may be hiding worry about exams, and asking about it before punishing.
In marriage: telling your husband 'I felt left out when you decided alone' instead of refusing to talk for three days.
In business: staying polite and firm with a customer who is haggling aggressively, so you keep both your price and your reputation.
In church, mosque or community groups: helping two members who have quarrelled to hear each other out.
With yourself: recognising when you need rest, and taking it without guilt.

Notice that none of these require a university degree, money or special equipment. They require attention, a few practised techniques and the willingness to try again when you get it wrong. That is exactly what the next 15 lessons will give you, one small skill at a time.

Explain why labelling a feeling helps you calm it

Many of us were raised to answer 'How are you?' with 'I'm fine' or 'Thank God'. That is polite, but inside it hides a lot. If you cannot name what you feel, you cannot manage it. This lesson gives you tools to name feelings accurately.
A woman sorting thoughts into groups
Sorting a jumble of feelings into clear names is the first step to handling them.
Why naming helps

Psychiatrist **Dan Siegel** sums this up as **'name it to tame it'**. Brain-imaging research at UCLA led by Matthew Lieberman (published in 2007) found that when people put their feelings into words, activity in the amygdala, a part of the brain linked to alarm and fear, went down. In plain terms: saying 'I feel anxious' to yourself is not weakness; it is already a step towards calm.
The Mood Meter

The **Yale Center for Emotional Intelligence** uses a simple tool called the **Mood Meter** in its RULER programme. You ask two questions: **How much energy do I have?** (high or low) and **How pleasant does this feel?** (pleasant or unpleasant). The answers place you in one of four colour zones.

Blue: low energy, unpleasant
Green: low energy, pleasant

No zone is bad. Red energy helps you rush a sick child to hospital. Blue feelings tell you that you have lost something that mattered. The aim is to know which zone you are in and whether it suits what you need to do next.
Go from vague to precise

Once you know your zone, look for the most exact word. 'Bad' could mean ashamed, lonely, guilty or overwhelmed, and each one needs a different response. Shame needs kindness to yourself; loneliness needs connection; being overwhelmed needs help or fewer tasks.

Listen to your body

Emotions show up in the body, often before you have words for them. Common signs include a tight chest or fast heartbeat (anxiety), a hot face or clenched fists (anger), a heavy body and slow movement (sadness), and loose shoulders with easy breathing (calm). Your own signs may differ. Learning them is like learning the warning lights on a car dashboard.
Worked example: unpacking 'I'm just tired'
For example, Aisha, a teacher in Kaduna, comes home and tells her husband she is 'just tired' and goes quiet all evening.
Energy check: low. Pleasantness: unpleasant. Zone: blue.
She asks herself what else is there. She remembers the head teacher criticised her lesson in front of colleagues.
Exact words: 'humiliated' and 'discouraged', not only 'tired'.
Body: heavy chest, no appetite.
Now she knows what she needs: to talk it through with someone she trusts and plan how to ask the head teacher for private feedback next time.
Naming the real feelings turned a silent evening into a short honest talk with her husband and a clear plan for the next day.
Use your own languages
Many Nigerian languages have rich words for feelings. If a Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo or Pidgin word fits better than an English one, use it. The goal is accuracy, not English.
Practise naming several times a day for a week. At first it feels slow. After a while you will start to notice feelings earlier, while they are still small.
Feelings often come mixed

You can feel two or more emotions at once. On the day your first child leaves for university you may feel proud (yellow), sad (blue) and worried about school fees (red) all together. Naming each part is more accurate than choosing one. It also stops you judging yourself: you are not 'confused', you are simply feeling several true things at the same time.

Some people find a **feelings wheel** helpful. One widely used version was created by Gloria Willcox in 1982. It places a few core feelings such as sad, mad, scared, joyful, peaceful and powerful in the centre, with more exact words spreading outwards. You can find free printable versions online and keep one on your phone.
A quick daily habit

When someone asks how you are and you answer 'fine', silently finish the sentence for yourself: 'Fine, but actually a bit anxious about rent.' You do not have to tell everyone, but you should tell yourself.

Emotions are not random. They are fast responses that prepare us to act. Fear prepares us to run or protect; anger prepares us to fight for something; sadness slows us down to recover. Understanding this chain helps you step in before a feeling turns into an action you regret.

The thought you add to a situation strongly shapes what you feel and do.

The key link is the **thought or interpretation**. Psychologists call this **appraisal**: the meaning you give to what happened. Two people can face the same situation and feel very differently, because they interpret it differently. This idea is also at the heart of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), a well-researched approach used by counsellors.

The urge is not the action

Every emotion comes with an **urge**: to shout, to hide, to cry, to eat, to check the phone again. An urge is not an order. Between the urge and the action there is a small gap. Emotional intelligence is the skill of widening that gap so you can choose. Viktor Frankl, a psychiatrist who survived Nazi concentration camps, wrote about the freedom to choose one's attitude even in terrible circumstances; this course builds on the same idea with daily practice.
Thoughts that pour fuel on the fire
**Mind-reading:** 'She thinks I am a failure.' (You do not actually know.)
**Always and never:** 'He never helps.' (Is it truly never?)
**Catastrophising:** 'If I lose this contract, my business is finished.'
**Labelling:** 'I am useless.' (One mistake does not make a person useless.)
**Should statements:** 'She should know I am tired.' (People cannot read minds.)
When you notice one of these, ask three questions: **What is the evidence? What else could explain this? What would I tell a friend who thought this?**
Worked example: the family WhatsApp group
For example, Funmi posts photos of her new tailoring shop on the family WhatsApp group. Two hours later, 14 people have seen it but only her aunt has replied.
Situation: few replies to her post.
First thought: 'Nobody in this family supports me.' Feeling: hurt (blue zone), with an urge to leave the group.
She checks the evidence: it is a weekday afternoon; most of her cousins work; her aunt did reply warmly.
Other explanations: people saw it while busy and plan to reply later; some rarely reply to anything.
New thought: 'People are busy. My aunt is proud of me.' Feeling: a little disappointed but calm.
Action: she leaves the group as it is and personally sends the photos to two cousins who might need clothes made.
By evening she has 9 replies and one cousin has booked a fitting. Leaving the group in anger would have cost her that customer.
Do not argue yourself out of real problems
Checking your thoughts is not the same as pretending everything is fine. If someone really is treating you badly, the goal is to see it clearly and respond wisely, not to explain it away.

A **trigger** is anything that sets off a strong emotional reaction, often bigger than the situation seems to deserve. Triggers can be words ('You are just like your mother'), tones of voice, situations (being kept waiting), places, dates, or body states such as hunger and tiredness. Knowing your triggers lets you prepare instead of being caught off guard.
A woman writing in a personal notebook
A trigger log turns surprise reactions into patterns you can plan for.
Why some things hit harder

Triggers often connect to something important to us: respect, fairness, safety, being valued, or an old hurt. If you grew up being compared to a sibling, a comment comparing you to a co-worker may sting much more than it would sting someone else. This is normal. The point is not to blame yourself but to understand yourself.
The HALT check

A simple check used in many self-help and recovery programmes is **HALT**: am I **H**ungry, **A**ngry, **L**onely or **T**ired? Any of these makes ordinary problems feel bigger. Many mothers who skip breakfast to get children to school find they are shortest-tempered by mid-morning. Sometimes the fix is a meal or a rest, not a difficult conversation.

For example, Blessing sells foodstuff at a market in Port Harcourt. She logs 11 strong reactions in one week.
She counts: 6 of the 11 happened before 10am.
5 of those 6 entries were marked 'hungry'.

The next week she logs 5 strong reactions instead of 11, and only 1 is about credit.
Write a trigger plan
Name the trigger: 'When I am kept waiting at the bank...'
Name your usual reaction: '...I become sharp with the staff.'
Plan ahead: 'I will go with a snack and something to read.'
Plan in the moment: 'I will notice my jaw tightening and take three slow breaths.'
Plan your words: 'Excuse me, please could you tell me roughly how long the wait is?'
When a trigger links to past trauma

If certain reminders bring back intense fear, flashbacks or panic connected to a frightening past experience, a trained counsellor, psychologist or doctor can help. You do not have to work through that alone with a notebook.
Positive patterns count too

Your log will also show moments that went well. If you handled a difficult customer calmly on Wednesday, write down what was different that day. Perhaps you had eaten, slept well or prayed before opening the shop. These are your **protective factors**, and you can plan to repeat them on purpose.

Share your patterns, if you wish, with one trusted person, such as a sister, friend or spouse. Tell them one trigger and how they can help, for example: 'If you see me getting sharp with the children in the morning, please remind me to eat something.' Many triggers become easier to handle when someone else knows about them and is on your side.
Review your log again after a month. Triggers can change as your life changes: a new job, a new baby or a move to a new city can bring new ones, and old ones can fade as you practise.

Finally, be patient with yourself. You will still react to triggers, especially when you are tired. Each time you notice a trigger, even after you have reacted, you are building the awareness that makes the next time easier. Progress looks like reacting a little less often, a little less strongly, and recovering a little faster.

**Self-regulation** means managing your emotions and impulses so that your actions match your values, even when you are upset. A **reaction** is fast and automatic: a shout, a slammed door, an angry voice note sent at midnight. A **response** is chosen. This lesson gives you tools to move from reacting to responding.

Flipping your lid

Psychiatrist Dan Siegel uses a simple **hand model of the brain**. Hold up your hand and fold your thumb into your palm, then fold your fingers over the thumb. Your wrist and palm stand for the deeper brain areas that handle alarm and survival. Your thumb stands for the emotional centre. Your fingers stand for the front of the brain (the prefrontal cortex) that plans, reasons and calms. When we are very upset, it is as if the fingers lift up: we **'flip our lid'** and the calm, thinking part loses its grip. The tools below help you fold the fingers back down.
STOP: a four-second pause
The STOP technique
Stop what you are doing
Take a slow breath
Observe body and thoughts
Proceed with a choice
STOP creates a short gap between the urge and the action.

STOP is a simple mindfulness tool. **Stop** (freeze your hands and mouth), **Take a breath** (one slow breath), **Observe** (what am I feeling, what am I about to do?) and **Proceed** (choose the action that fits your values). It takes less than ten seconds and you can do it in the middle of a conversation.
Box breathing
Breathe in slowly through your nose for a count of 4.
Hold your breath gently for a count of 4.
Breathe out slowly through your mouth for a count of 4.
Hold empty for a count of 4.
Repeat 4 times. If holding feels uncomfortable, skip the holds and just make the out-breath longer than the in-breath.

Slow breathing, especially a long out-breath, activates the body's calming system and slows the heart rate. That is why it works quickly, whether you are about to address a meeting or about to shout at a child.
5-4-3-2-1 grounding

When worry is racing, bring your attention back to the present by naming: **5** things you can see, **4** things you can touch, **3** things you can hear, **2** things you can smell and **1** thing you can taste. In a market, that might be: tomatoes, a red umbrella, the scale, a customer's blue wrapper, a bus; your stool, the money pouch, a nylon bag, your wrapper; a hawker's call, a radio, a horn; pepper, fuel; the sweet in your mouth.
Worked example: the school fees call

For example, Chioma, a civil servant in Enugu, gets a call from her son's school at work: fees are overdue and he may be sent home tomorrow. Her face goes hot and she wants to call her husband and shout.
Stop: she puts the phone face down and does not dial.
Takes a breath: 4 rounds of box breathing at her desk, about one minute.
Observes: 'I am scared and embarrassed (red zone). I am telling myself he forgot on purpose.'
Proceeds: she calls the bursar first and asks if she can pay half (for example, N60,000 of N120,000, approximate figures) today and the rest within two weeks.
Then she calls her husband: 'The school called about fees. I have arranged to pay half today. Can we sit down tonight and plan the rest?'
Her son stays in school, and the evening is a planning talk instead of a fight.

Practise when calm
These tools work best if you practise them when you are calm, for example box breathing for two minutes each morning. Then your body knows what to do when stress hits.
Repair when you slip

You will not always catch yourself. When you do react badly, repair quickly. Go back, own your part and name what you will do differently: 'I am sorry I shouted this morning. I was stressed about money, but that is not your fault. Next time I will take a breath before I speak.' Repair teaches children and adults that relationships can survive mistakes, and it shows you are serious about change. Self-regulation is not perfection; it is noticing sooner and recovering faster each time.

Anger is a normal, healthy emotion. It tells you that something feels unfair or that a boundary has been crossed. The problem is not anger itself but what we do with it. The American Psychological Association describes three main approaches: **expressing** anger in an assertive, not aggressive, way; **suppressing** it and redirecting it; and **calming** yourself inside. Suppressing anger for a long time without dealing with it can turn into resentment, so the healthiest path is usually calm, honest expression.

Say it with an 'I' statement

An 'I' statement describes your feeling and need without attacking. The pattern is: **'I feel [emotion] when [specific behaviour], because [reason]. I would like [request].'** Compare 'You are so careless, you never lock the shop!' with 'I feel worried when the shop is left unlocked, because we could lose our stock. Please could you lock it and send me a text when you leave?'

Stress is the body's response to demands. Short bursts can help you meet a deadline. Long-term stress with no recovery can harm sleep, mood and health. The World Health Organization's free guide **'Doing What Matters in Times of Stress'** teaches skills such as grounding, unhooking from difficult thoughts, and acting on your values. It is available as a free download.
Worked example: the month-end squeeze
For example, Zainab, a hairdresser in Abuja, has rent due on Friday, two clients who have not paid, and a sick mother. She cannot sleep.
She writes every worry on paper: 8 items.
She sorts them: 4 she can act on (call the two clients, ask her landlord for one week, book her mother a clinic visit, ask her sister to share the clinic costs).
4 she cannot control (fuel price, her mother's illness itself, the landlord's mood, a slow month).
She schedules the 4 actions: 2 calls at 9am, landlord at 11am, clinic booking at noon.
For the rest she does 5 minutes of slow breathing at night and reminds herself, 'I have done what I can today.'
By Thursday one client has paid N15,000 (approximate), the landlord agrees to 5 extra days, and her sister pays half of the clinic visit. She sleeps better because her worries have a plan.
When anger becomes dangerous

If you or someone at home is being hit, threatened or controlled, this is not an anger-management problem to fix with breathing. Your safety comes first: go to a safe place, contact trusted family, the police or an organisation that supports women. In Nigeria, the Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Act 2015 makes domestic violence an offence.
A daily stress-care routine
**Sleep:** aim for a regular bedtime; put the phone away 30 minutes before.
**Move:** a 20-minute brisk walk, dancing or chores done briskly.
**Eat:** regular meals; avoid going long hours without food.
**Connect:** one real conversation a day with someone who cares about you.
**Pause:** two minutes of box breathing or quiet prayer, morning and night.

Watch also for **displaced anger**, when frustration from one place lands on someone else. A hard day with a rude customer can come out as shouting at the house help or the children. When you notice this, say so honestly: 'I am upset about something at the shop, not about you.' Naming it often lowers the heat for everyone in the room.
Anger is a signal; express it assertively, not aggressively.
Catch anger low on the ladder; take a time-out at level 7 or above.
'I feel... when... because... I would like...' keeps conversations safe.
Act on what you control, accept what you cannot, and care for your body daily.

Agree a time-out signal with one family member and write it down.

Carrying sadness, grief and disappointment
Explain why sadness is a normal and useful emotion

Use practical self-care and support steps during loss

Sadness tells us we have lost something that mattered: a person, a hope, a relationship, a business, our health, or a plan for the future. Many women are taught to 'be strong' and carry on as if nothing happened. Being strong does not mean not feeling. Allowing sadness, and getting support, usually helps people recover better than pushing it down.
A woman sitting alone feeling sad
Sadness is a natural response to loss, and it deserves care rather than shame.
Different kinds of loss
**Bereavement:** the death of a loved one.
**Disappointment:** a failed exam, a contract you did not win, a visa refused, a business that closed.
**Relationship loss:** separation, divorce, a friendship that ended, children moving away.
**Hidden losses:** miscarriage, infertility, loss of health or of a role, which others may not see or talk about.
Grief moves back and forth

You may have heard of the 'five stages of grief' (denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance), first described by Elisabeth Kubler-Ross. Kubler-Ross herself later explained that these are not fixed steps in order. People can feel several at once, move back and forth, or skip some. Another well-known idea, the **Dual Process Model** by Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut, describes healthy grieving as moving between two kinds of activity: facing the loss (crying, remembering, talking about the person) and restoring life (sorting finances, caring for children, returning to work). Both are normal, and switching between them is healthy.
Moving between loss and restoring
Facing the loss
Taking a break
Rebuilding daily life
Remembering again
Healthy grief swings between facing the loss and getting on with life.
What helps
**Allow the feeling.** Set aside time to cry, pray or remember, instead of fighting it all day.
**Keep the basics.** Small meals, water, some sleep, a short walk. Grief is tiring for the body.
**Accept practical help.** Let people cook, watch children or run errands. Tell them exactly what helps.
**Talk to someone safe.** A friend, sister, faith leader or support group.
**Keep simple routines.** Waking time, prayers, one small task, so the day has shape.
**Delay big decisions** such as selling a house or moving, if you can, until the first wave has passed.
Worked example: after a business closes
For example, Grace ran a small restaurant in Ibadan for four years. After rent and food prices rose, she closed it. For weeks she stays in bed and tells friends, 'I am fine.'
She names her feelings: grief, shame and fear about money (blue and red zones).
She allows them: 20 minutes each evening to write about what she misses and what she learned.
She keeps basics: a walk to the market every morning to buy food for the house.
She accepts help: her friend reviews her accounts with her and they find she can sell her freezer and chairs for about N450,000 (approximate).
After six weeks, when she feels steadier, she starts a small home-cooking order service through WhatsApp, using the lessons from the restaurant.
Grace still feels sad about the restaurant at times, but she is working again and the sadness no longer controls her day.
Supporting someone who is grieving
Say the person's name and share a memory; many grieving people want the person remembered.
Offer specific help: 'I will bring soup on Tuesday,' not 'Call me if you need anything.'
Avoid phrases that close the conversation, like 'At least...' or 'Stop crying, it is God's will.'
Keep checking in after the burial; loneliness often grows when visitors stop coming.
When to get professional help

Sadness after loss is normal. Please see a doctor, counsellor or mental health professional if low mood lasts most days for more than two weeks, if you cannot eat, sleep or care for yourself or your children, if you feel hopeless, or if you have any thoughts of harming yourself. If you feel unsafe right now, go to the nearest hospital emergency unit or tell someone close to you immediately.

Remember that disappointment, even without a death, can bring real grief. Not getting a job, a pregnancy that did not happen, or a child who chose a different path can all deserve the same gentleness. Give yourself permission to feel it without comparing your loss to anyone else's.

Faith, culture and family traditions can be a real comfort during grief: prayers, the gathering of relatives, songs and remembrance events. Use what helps you. At the same time, it is fine to tell relatives gently if some customs feel too heavy right now, or if you need quiet rather than visitors.

Grief also has no fixed timetable. Anniversaries, festive seasons and family events can bring strong waves of sadness even years later. Plan for these days: let someone know, keep the day lighter and include a small act of remembrance.
Sadness signals loss and deserves care, not shame.
Grief does not follow neat stages; it moves back and forth.
Healthy grieving mixes facing the loss with rebuilding daily life.
Lasting hopelessness or thoughts of self-harm need professional help now.

**Resilience** is the ability to adapt and recover when life gets hard: a job loss, illness, a failed business, family conflict, or the daily pressure of rising prices. The American Psychological Association describes resilience not as a fixed trait but as something built from behaviours, thoughts and actions that anyone can learn. Resilient people still feel pain. They simply find ways to keep going and grow.
A small green seedling
Like a seedling pushing through soil, resilience grows a little at a time.
Four pillars of resilience
The APA guide on building resilience groups helpful practices into four areas. Here they are in everyday terms.
Pillar

The three Ps: how you explain setbacks

Psychologist Martin Seligman, known for his work on optimism, found that how people explain bad events to themselves affects how quickly they recover. He described three patterns, often called the three Ps:
**Personal:** 'It is all my fault.' versus 'Several things caused this, including some I could not control.'
**Pervasive:** 'My whole life is ruined.' versus 'This affects one area; other parts of my life are still good.'
**Permanent:** 'It will always be like this.' versus 'This is hard now, and it will change.'
Worked example: the rejected loan
For example, Amaka applies for a N500,000 (approximate) business loan from a microfinance bank to buy a second sewing machine and is turned down.
First thoughts: 'I am not good at business (personal). Nothing works for me (pervasive). I will never grow (permanent).'
Personal, reframed: she asks the loan officer why. The reason: no 6-month bank statement showing regular sales. That is fixable.
Pervasive, reframed: her customers are happy, her children are well, she has a supportive sister.
Permanent, reframed: 'If I put all my sales through my Moniepoint account for 6 months, I can reapply.'
Connection: she joins a weekly ajo contribution with 9 other traders as a second path to the money.
Six months later she has a clear sales record and her ajo payout is due. A setback became a plan with two routes.
Small daily habits that build resilience
**Three good things:** each night, write three things that went well and why. Seligman's research team tested this exercise.
**One small step:** when a problem feels huge, ask 'What is one thing I can do today?'
**Look after your body:** sleep, regular meals and movement make setbacks easier to carry.
**Help someone else:** helping others is one of the APA's suggested ways to build a sense of purpose.
**Remember past survival:** list hard times you have already come through and what got you through.
Resilience is not doing everything alone

Asking for help is part of resilience, not a failure of it. Women who carry a household often think they must manage everything. Sharing the load with family, friends, your cooperative or a professional is a strong choice.

Resilience also grows from **flexible coping**: knowing when to push forward and when to rest, when to solve a problem and when to accept something you cannot change. A trader who cannot afford new stock this month might focus on serving loyal customers well and saving a little each day, instead of borrowing at a high interest rate in panic. Choosing the response that fits the situation is itself a resilience skill.

Finally, notice that resilience is shared. Families, cooperatives and women's networks such as the WODDI Good Mother Network are sources of strength. When you support another woman through her setback, you also strengthen your own sense of connection and purpose.
Review your plan every few months. As you notice which tools help most, keep them close, for example as a note on your phone you can open on a hard day.

Understanding Others' Emotions

Turn your attention outward. You will learn what real empathy is (and how it differs from sympathy), how to read faces, voices and silences with care, how small daily habits protect relationships, and how to coach your children through their big feelings.
Empathy: seeing through someone else's eyes
Distinguish cognitive, emotional and compassionate empathy
Explain the difference between empathy and sympathy
Use reflective listening to show you understand
Avoid common responses that shut people down

**Empathy** is the ability to understand and share another person's feelings and point of view. It is one of Goleman's five areas and the bridge between managing yourself and relating well to others. Empathy does not mean agreeing with everything someone says or does. It means understanding their experience well enough to respond with care.
Two people hugging
Empathy says 'I am with you', even when you cannot fix the problem.
Three kinds of empathy
Psychologists Daniel Goleman and Paul Ekman describe three kinds of empathy. You need all three.
Type
What it is
Example
Cognitive empathy
Understanding how someone thinks and sees the situation
'She is worried her boss will think she is lazy.'
Emotional empathy
Feeling something of what they feel
Your own chest tightens as your friend describes her fear
Compassionate empathy (empathic concern)
Understanding, feeling and being moved to help
You offer to sit with her while she calls the hospital

Too little emotional empathy can make you seem cold. Too much, with no boundaries, can leave you drained, especially for nurses, teachers, carers and mothers. Compassionate empathy balances the two: you care, and you also stay steady enough to help.
Empathy versus sympathy

Researcher **Brené Brown** explains the difference in a short animated talk for the RSA. Sympathy looks down at someone from a distance ('Oh, poor you') and often tries to find a silver lining ('At least...'). Empathy climbs down into the hole with them: 'I know what it is like down here, and you are not alone.'
Sympathy or empathy?
Sympathy

Reflective listening: show you understand
**Give full attention.** Put the phone face down. Turn your body towards the person.
**Listen for feelings and facts.** What happened? How do they feel about it?
**Reflect back.** 'So you have been doing the work of two people since Bisi left, and you feel exhausted and unappreciated.'
**Check.** 'Have I understood that right?'
**Ask before advising.** 'Would you like ideas, or do you mostly need to talk?'
Worked example: the friend who lost her job
For example, Halima tells her friend Joy on the phone that her company in Lagos has just laid off 20 staff, including her.
Unhelpful response: 'At least you got a severance package. You will find another job, don't worry.'
Joy gives full attention: she steps away from the TV.
She reflects: 'Eight years there, and they told you by email. You must be shocked and worried about the children's fees.'
Halima says, 'Yes, and embarrassed. I don't know how to tell my mother.'
Joy asks: 'Do you want to think through what to say to her, or do you just need to vent tonight?' Halima chooses to vent tonight and plan tomorrow.
Halima feels understood, and the next day they draft her CV together. Joy helped more by listening first than by rushing to reassure.
Responses that block empathy
**Minimising:** 'It's not that serious.'
**One-upping:** 'You think that is bad? Let me tell you what happened to me.'
**Quick fixing:** jumping to advice before the person feels heard.
**Spiritual bypassing:** 'Just pray about it' as a way of ending the conversation. Prayer can be a real comfort; offer it alongside listening, not instead of it.
Empathy for people you disagree with

Try cognitive empathy with someone who annoys you, such as a demanding customer or in-law. Ask silently: 'What might she be worried about? What does she need?' You do not have to agree, but understanding her need often shows you a better way to respond.
Protect yourself from empathy fatigue

Women are often the people everyone brings their problems to: the sister who listens, the friend who advises, the mother who absorbs everyone's moods. Feeling other people's pain all day without rest can lead to exhaustion, sometimes called **empathy fatigue** or compassion fatigue, which is common among health workers and carers. Signs include feeling numb, irritable, or dreading other people's calls.
**Notice your limit:** 'I can listen for 15 minutes tonight, then I need to sleep.'
**Separate their feeling from yours:** 'This is her sadness. I can care without carrying it all.'
**Refill yourself:** rest, prayer, laughter and time with people who also listen to you.
**Share the load:** you do not have to be the only support. Encourage her to talk to others too, including professionals where needed.
Empathy is a strength that lasts longest when it is balanced with boundaries.
Like every skill in this course, empathy improves with practice. Start with one conversation a day where your only goal is to understand, not to fix or win.

Reading faces, voices and silences
Notice facial, vocal and body cues of emotion
Interpret cues with cultural awareness and without jumping to conclusions
Read emotional cues in WhatsApp and phone communication
Check your reading with a gentle question

Much of what people feel is shown, not said. Tone of voice, facial expression, posture and even silence carry emotional messages. Reading these cues accurately is the first ability in the Mayer and Salovey model, applied to other people. It helps you respond to what someone really needs, not only to their words.
Two people in conversation
Watching the face and listening to the tone tells you more than words alone.
Three channels to watch
Channel
What to notice
Possible meanings
Face
Eyes, brows, mouth, sudden changes
Tight lips may show anger or holding back; a forced smile may hide hurt
Voice
Speed, loudness, pitch, pauses
Fast and loud may mean anxiety or anger; flat and slow may mean sadness or tiredness
Body
Posture, hands, distance, eye contact
Crossed arms may mean defensiveness or simply cold; turning away may mean discomfort

Psychologist Paul Ekman's research found some facial expressions of basic emotions, such as happiness, sadness, anger, fear, surprise and disgust, are recognised across many cultures. But how much people show, and in which situations, depends strongly on culture, family and personality.
Read cues in context
**Culture:** in many Nigerian families, a younger person avoids direct eye contact with an elder as a sign of respect, not dishonesty.
**Clusters, not single signs:** one crossed arm means little. Crossed arms, a short reply and looking away together tell you more.
**Change from normal:** notice when someone who is usually chatty goes quiet. A change from their usual pattern is often the strongest clue.
**Situation:** a sharp tone in a hot, crowded bus may be about the heat, not about you.

Look at face, voice, body
Look for a cluster
Compare with their normal
Consider culture and situation
Ask gently to check
A good reading is a guess you check, not a judgement.
Reading cues in messages

On WhatsApp and SMS you lose face and voice, so misreadings are common. A short 'Ok.' can feel cold, but the sender may just be busy or driving. Clues in messages include sudden changes in length, missing greetings when they normally greet, delayed replies compared with usual, and voice notes where you can hear tone. When a message worries you, call or send a voice note instead of guessing. Never assume the worst from punctuation alone.
Worked example: the quiet staff member

For example, Ronke runs a small catering business in Abeokuta with 4 staff. Usually her assistant, Tolu, jokes while cooking. For three days Tolu has been quiet, working fast, avoiding eye contact and leaving on time exactly.
Cluster: quiet, avoiding eye contact, leaving promptly.
Change from normal: very different from her usual cheerful self.
Ronke avoids guessing ('She is lazy now' or 'She wants to quit').
She asks privately: 'Tolu, you have seemed quieter this week. Is everything okay? No pressure, I just noticed.'
Tolu shares that her mother is in hospital and she is rushing to visit after work.
Ronke allows her to leave 30 minutes early for two weeks. Tolu stays, and her loyalty to the business grows.
Check gently

Your reading is a guess. Check it with a tentative, open question that leaves room for the person to say no: 'You seem a bit tense, am I right?' or 'I may be wrong, but you sound disappointed.' Avoid accusing statements like 'Why are you angry with me?', which can make someone defensive even if they were not angry.
Respect privacy

Noticing someone's feelings does not give you the right to push. If they say 'I'm fine' after you have asked gently, accept it and let them know the door is open: 'Okay. If you want to talk later, I am here.'
Listening to what is not said

Silence can mean many things: thinking, respect, discomfort, sadness, anger, or simply tiredness. In many homes, a wife or daughter-in-law may stay silent to keep peace while feeling hurt inside. A child may go quiet rather than say they are being bullied. Do not treat silence as agreement. If something important was discussed and someone said nothing, follow up later in private: 'You were quiet when we talked about the move. What do you think about it?'

Also read your own cues. If you notice you are speaking fast, frowning or folding your arms, others are reading those signals too. A relaxed face, an open posture and a calm voice invite people to share. Before an important conversation, take a breath and soften your shoulders so your body says the same thing as your words.
With practice, reading cues becomes quicker and more accurate. Keep checking your guesses, and you will learn the particular signals of the people closest to you.

Strengthening relationships with everyday EQ
Recognise and respond to 'bids' for connection
Name the Four Horsemen that damage relationships and their antidotes
Use a gentle start-up to raise a complaint
Make and accept repair attempts after conflict

Relationships with friends, siblings, in-laws, neighbours and colleagues are built in small moments. Psychologist **John Gottman** and his colleagues have studied couples and families for decades at what is now The Gottman Institute. Many of their findings apply to any close relationship, and they give us clear, practical habits.
Friends standing together
Strong friendships are built from many small moments of attention.
Bids for connection

A **bid** is any attempt to get attention, interest or support: 'Look at this video,' 'My back is paining me,' a sigh, a touch. You can respond in three ways: **turn towards** (show interest), **turn away** (ignore, keep scrolling) or **turn against** (respond with irritation). Gottman's research found that people in lasting relationships turned towards each other's bids far more often than people whose relationships ended.
The Four Horsemen and their antidotes
Gottman named four communication patterns that strongly predict relationship breakdown, and he called them the Four Horsemen. Each has an antidote.
Horseman
What it sounds like
Antidote
Criticism (attacking character)
'You are so selfish, you never think of anyone.'
Gentle start-up
'I felt left out when you made plans without asking me. Can we plan together next time?'
Contempt (mocking, eye-rolling, insults)
'Who even taught you to cook?'
Build appreciation
Regularly say what you value and respect
Defensiveness (excuses, counter-attack)
'It's not my fault, you did worse!'
Take responsibility
'You are right, I forgot. I'm sorry.'
Stonewalling (shutting down, silent treatment)
Walking away, refusing to speak for days
Self-soothe and return
'I'm overwhelmed. Give me 20 minutes and we will talk.'

Gottman identified **contempt** as the strongest predictor of breakup of the four. It communicates disgust and superiority. If you notice contempt in yourself, it is a sign you need to rebuild appreciation.
A gentle start-up
Start with 'I feel'
Describe the situation
Avoid blame words
State a positive need
How a difficult conversation starts usually decides how it ends.
The 5 to 1 ratio

In Gottman's studies, stable couples had about **five positive interactions for every negative one** during conflict. Positive interactions include showing interest, a kind word, humour, affection and agreement. This does not mean avoiding all criticism. It means making sure warmth far outweighs tension.
Worked example: two sisters and the family business
For example, Ijeoma and her younger sister Nneka run a cosmetics stall together in Aba. Ijeoma is upset that Nneka arrives late most days.
Old way (criticism): 'You are so unserious. You are always late and I do all the work.' Nneka becomes defensive and they argue in front of customers.
New way, gentle start-up, in private: 'I feel stressed when I open alone, because the morning rush is our busiest hour. Could you be here by 8am, or can we agree which days you open?'
Nneka explains she has been taking their mother to the clinic twice a week.
Ijeoma takes responsibility: 'I didn't know. I'm sorry I assumed.'
They agree: Nneka opens on Monday, Wednesday and Friday; Ijeoma on clinic days.
The problem is solved in ten minutes, and the sisters avoid a quarrel that could have damaged both the business and their relationship.
Repair attempts

A **repair attempt** is anything that stops tension from rising: a joke, a touch, 'Let me try again,' 'I see your point.' Every relationship has conflict. What matters most is whether repair attempts are made and accepted. When someone offers a repair, try to accept it, even if you are still a little upset.
When a relationship is harmful

These tools are for relationships where both people are basically safe and respectful. If someone repeatedly insults, threatens, controls or harms you, the problem is not your communication. Seek support from trusted people, a counsellor or an organisation that helps women.
Appreciation as a daily habit

Appreciation is the main antidote to contempt, and it works in every relationship. Make it specific: not just 'thank you', but 'thank you for picking the children up today, it gave me time to finish my orders.' Specific thanks show you noticed the effort. Try to catch people doing something right at least once a day: your spouse, a colleague, an apprentice, a child.
Send a short WhatsApp voice note to a friend saying one thing you value about her.

Emotion coaching for mothers and caregivers
Describe the five steps of emotion coaching
Validate a child's feelings while still setting limits on behaviour
Help children name feelings at different ages

Children are not born knowing how to manage feelings. They learn mostly from the adults around them: how we react when they cry, how we handle our own anger, and whether feelings are talked about at home. John Gottman's research with families, described in his book *Raising an Emotionally Intelligent Child*, found that parents who coach children through emotions help them manage feelings and get along better with others.
A mother caring for her child
Children learn to handle feelings by watching and being guided by the adults who care for them.
Feelings are allowed; some behaviour is not

The core idea of emotion coaching is simple: **all feelings are acceptable, but not all behaviour is.** A child may feel angry that his brother took his toy. Hitting is not allowed. When we punish the feeling ('Stop crying or I will give you something to cry about'), children learn to hide feelings rather than manage them. When we accept the feeling and guide the behaviour, they learn self-regulation.
The five steps of emotion coaching
Gottman's five steps
Notice the emotion
See a chance to connect
Listen and validate
Help name it
Set limits, solve problems
Each step builds on the one before.
**Be aware of the child's emotion,** especially when it is still small.
**See it as a chance** to connect and teach, not as a nuisance.
**Listen with empathy and validate:** 'You are upset because you wanted to go with Daddy.'
**Help the child name the feeling:** 'Are you feeling disappointed? Jealous? Scared?'
**Set limits and solve the problem together:** 'It's okay to be angry, but we don't hit. What could you do next time your brother takes your toy?'
Worked example: the 6-year-old at the party
For example, Bukola takes her 6-year-old daughter, Dami, to a cousin's birthday. When the cake is cut, Dami screams and throws her plate because she did not get the piece with the candle.
Notice: Bukola sees Dami's face crumple before the plate is thrown and kneels down to her level.
Connect: instead of shouting, she takes Dami's hand and moves her a few steps away from the crowd.
Validate: 'You really wanted the piece with the candle. That is disappointing.'
Name: 'Are you feeling disappointed and a bit jealous?' Dami nods, crying.
Limits and problem-solving: 'It is okay to feel disappointed. Throwing plates is not okay. Let's pick up the plate together. Next time, what can you do when you feel this way?' Dami says, 'Tell you.'
Dami calms in about 3 minutes, helps clean up and goes back to play. She has learned a word for her feeling and a better action, instead of only learning that she is 'bad'.

Age
2 to 4 years
Simple words: happy, sad, angry, scared. Point to faces in picture books.
5 to 8 years

Your emotions matter too

Caregivers cannot pour from an empty cup. Mothers, grandmothers and other carers often go without rest, help or time for themselves. Tiredness and stress make it much harder to stay calm with children. Use the tools from Module 2 on yourself: notice your HALT signs, take a breath before responding, share tasks with your partner or family, and repair if you shout.
Never use fear or harsh physical punishment to stop feelings

UNICEF and the World Health Organization recommend positive, non-violent discipline. If you are worried that a child's anger, fear or sadness is very intense, lasting a long time, or affecting school, eating or sleep, speak to a doctor or school counsellor. If you ever feel close to losing control with a child, put the child somewhere safe, step away, and call someone you trust.
Modelling: children copy what we do

Children learn as much from watching you manage your own feelings as from anything you say. When you are upset, you can narrate your coping out loud: 'Mummy is feeling frustrated because the light went off while I was cooking. I'm going to take three deep breaths and then light the gas.' This teaches them that adults have feelings too, and shows them exactly what to do.

When you lose your temper, repair with the child: 'I'm sorry I shouted. I was tired, but it was not your fault. I love you.' Some parents worry that apologising to a child weakens their authority. In practice, it teaches responsibility and makes children feel safe. Over time, children who are coached in this way begin to use the same words with their siblings and friends.

Whether you work in an office, a school, a hospital, or run your own stall, salon or online shop, work is full of emotions: pressure from bosses, demanding customers, difficult colleagues, money worries. Goleman's original writing on emotional intelligence focused on the workplace, arguing that self-awareness, self-regulation, empathy and social skills matter alongside technical skill, especially for people who lead others.
A smiling customer at a shop
Customers remember how you made them feel, especially when something went wrong.
Handling an upset customer: LAST
**LAST** is a simple service-recovery method used in hospitality and customer service: **Listen, Apologise, Solve, Thank.**
The LAST method
Listen fully
Apologise sincerely
Solve the problem
Thank the customer
Calming the feeling first makes solving the problem much easier.
**Listen** without interrupting. Let the customer finish. Nod, keep a calm face, and reflect: 'So the gown was not ready on Saturday as promised, and you had to wear something else to the wedding.'
**Apologise** for their experience, sincerely and without excuses: 'I am truly sorry. That must have been very frustrating.'
**Solve:** offer a clear fix or choice: 'I can finish it today by 5pm and give you N3,000 (approximate) off, or refund your deposit. Which do you prefer?'
**Thank** them: 'Thank you for telling me directly. It helps me improve.'
Worked example: the angry online order

For example, Patience sells hair products on Instagram from Benin City. A customer sends an angry voice note: her order of 3 bottles of hair oil (about N12,000 total, approximate) arrived with one bottle broken, and she calls Patience 'a scammer'.
Patience feels insulted (red zone). She uses STOP and waits 10 minutes before replying.
Listen: she replies, 'I hear you. You paid for 3 bottles and one arrived broken. That is very disappointing.'
Apologise: 'I am sorry this happened.' She does not argue about the word 'scammer'.
Solve: 'Please send me a photo of the broken bottle. I will send a replacement with my rider tomorrow at no cost, and I will pack in bubble wrap from now on.'
Thank: 'Thank you for letting me know quickly.'
The replacement costs her about N4,000 plus delivery (approximate). The customer leaves a positive review and orders again the next month.
Giving feedback: the SBI model

The **Situation, Behaviour, Impact (SBI)** model, developed by the Center for Creative Leadership, keeps feedback specific and fair. Describe the **situation** (when and where), the **behaviour** (what the person did, not your judgement of them), and the **impact** (the effect). Then invite their view.
Unhelpful
SBI version
'You are careless with customers.'
'At the shop on Tuesday afternoon (S), when the woman asked about prices, you kept looking at your phone (B). She left without buying, and we may have lost a regular customer (I). What happened?'
'Well done.'
'In this morning's meeting (S), you explained the new price list clearly (B). Everyone understood and there were no questions afterwards (I). Thank you.'
Receiving criticism
Breathe and listen to the end before responding.
Ask for specifics: 'Can you give me an example?'
Separate the message from the delivery. Even if it was said harshly, is there something useful in it?
Thank the person, and take time to think if you need it: 'Let me reflect on that and come back to you tomorrow.'
Emotions and business decisions

Strong emotions can push poor decisions: panic-buying stock when prices rise, saying yes to every credit request out of guilt, or making a big investment because a friend made you feel excited. Before any decision involving significant money, check your zone. If you are in the red or very high yellow zone, wait 24 hours, write down the numbers and, if possible, talk to someone you trust.
Scams play on emotions

Many scams are designed to make you feel fear ('Your account will be blocked'), greed ('Double your money in 7 days') or urgency ('Pay now or lose the offer'). A strong rush of emotion around money is a signal to slow down. Never share your BVN, card PIN or OTP with anyone who contacts you, and check directly with your bank using the official number.

Your own wellbeing at work matters too. If you notice you are dreading work every day, feeling exhausted even after rest, or becoming cynical about customers or colleagues, these can be signs of burnout. Talk to your manager about workload if you are employed, share tasks or close one day a week if you run your own business, and see a doctor if the exhaustion continues.

EQ in marriage and partnership

Handle conflict using a gentle start-up, breaks and compromise

Marriage and long-term partnership bring two people, often two families, and sometimes two cultures together. Money, children, in-laws, roles at home and faith can all become sources of tension. Emotional intelligence will not remove disagreement, but it changes how couples move through it. Many of the most practical ideas come from John Gottman's research with couples, introduced in Module 3.
A couple standing together
Small daily habits of attention and respect protect a marriage through hard seasons.
Love maps: know your partner's world

Gottman uses the term **love map** for how well you know your partner's inner world: their worries, hopes, friends, stresses at work and dreams. Couples with detailed love maps cope better with stressful events like a new baby or a job loss. You build a love map by asking open questions and remembering the answers.
'What is worrying you most at work right now?'
'If money were not a problem, what would you love to do?'
'What was the best part of your week?'
'Is there anything I do that makes you feel really appreciated?'
Handling conflict well
Healthy conflict checklist
Choose a calm time
Start gently
Take breaks if flooded
Accept repair attempts
Look for compromise
These five habits keep disagreements from turning into lasting damage.

Gottman describes **flooding**: when your heart is racing and you feel overwhelmed, you cannot listen well. If either of you is flooded, take a break of at least 20 minutes, calm your body, and come back. Do not use the break to plan your next attack.
Solvable problems and lasting differences

Gottman's research found that a large share of couple conflicts are about **perpetual problems**: ongoing differences in personality, values or habits that may never fully go away. One may be a saver and one a spender; one may want to visit family every weekend and the other prefer rest. The goal with these is not to 'win', but to understand the dream or need behind each position and find a way to live with the difference. **Solvable problems**, like who takes the children to school on Mondays, can be fixed with a clear agreement.
Worked example: money and the extended family
For example, Adaeze and her husband Tunde both work in Lagos. Tunde regularly sends money to his younger brothers, and Adaeze feels the household is being left short. They argue every month.
Adaeze chooses a calm Saturday morning and starts gently: 'I feel anxious about our savings when large amounts go out without us planning. Can we sit down with the numbers together?'
Tunde explains the need behind his position: as the first son, supporting his brothers' school fees matters deeply to him and to his late father's memory.
Adaeze shares hers: security for their own children and an emergency fund.
They write their monthly income (for example, N650,000 combined, approximate) and agree a fixed family-support amount of N80,000 per month, plus N50,000 into savings first.
They agree to review it every 3 months and to discuss any extra request above N20,000 together first.
The difference in values remains, but the monthly fight stops because they have a shared plan that respects both needs.
Everyday habits that protect a marriage
Turn towards bids: answer when your partner shares something, even briefly.
Say thank you for ordinary things: cooking, fixing the generator, school runs.
Spend 20 minutes a day talking about something other than bills and children.
Share the load at home openly; unspoken resentment about chores builds up.
Keep private disagreements private, not in front of relatives or on social media.
When it is not safe

Communication tools are for relationships where both people are safe. Hitting, threats, forced sex, controlling all the money, cutting you off from family, or constant insults are abuse, not a communication problem. You deserve safety. Reach out to trusted family, a faith leader, a lawyer, the police or an organisation that supports women. In Nigeria, the Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Act 2015 provides legal protection against domestic violence.

Couples counselling, through a trained counsellor or a well-prepared faith-based marriage counsellor, can help when the same arguments keep repeating. Seeking help early, before resentment hardens, is a sign of commitment, not failure.

If you are single, widowed or separated, these skills still apply: to a future partnership, to co-parenting with a former partner, and to close relationships with siblings and friends. Co-parenting in particular goes better when both parents keep conversations about the children calm, brief and focused on the children's needs rather than on old hurts.

Many women lead without a formal title: as a women's group chair, a cooperative secretary, a church or mosque coordinator, a market association leader, a school PTA member or a family elder. Leading people means handling their emotions as well as tasks. Groups do better when the leader stays calm, listens well and treats people fairly.

A leader's mood spreads through the group, for better or for worse.

In a well-known Harvard Business Review article, *Leadership That Gets Results* (2000), Goleman described six leadership styles, each drawing on different emotional intelligence skills. Good leaders switch between them depending on the situation.

Each tells their side
Reflect feelings and needs
Find shared goals
Agree clear next steps
A calm, fair process helps both people feel respected.
Worked example: the cooperative contribution dispute

For example, Folake chairs a 20-member women's thrift cooperative in Ilorin. Two members, Mama Sade and Kafayat, quarrel publicly in the WhatsApp group: Kafayat says Mama Sade collected her payout early and has missed two contributions of N10,000 each (approximate).
Folake posts in the group: 'Let us not discuss this here. I will meet both of you on Saturday.' She takes the conversation out of public view.
At the meeting she sets rules: one person speaks at a time, no insults.
Each tells her side. Folake reflects: 'Kafayat, you feel it is unfair because you have paid every week. Mama Sade, you are embarrassed because your shop was closed for a month after flooding.'
Shared goal: both want the cooperative to survive and stay trusted.
Agreement: Mama Sade pays the N20,000 in four weekly instalments of N5,000, recorded by the treasurer. Folake proposes a clear written rule for missed payments at the next meeting.
The group calms down, the missing money is repaid within a month, and the new written rule prevents future quarrels.
Staying steady under public pressure
Do not reply to provocation in a group chat while angry. Wait, then reply briefly and calmly, or move the conversation to private.
Separate the person from the problem: criticise ideas and actions, never someone's family or character.
Admit mistakes openly. A leader who says 'I got that wrong, here is how I will fix it' builds trust.
Protect confidentiality: what members share privately should not become gossip.
Lead by example
Members copy the leader. If you greet people warmly, listen without interrupting and stay calm during disagreements, the group slowly does the same.
Motivating volunteers

Most community groups run on volunteers, who give their time without pay. People stay involved when they feel valued, see that their work makes a difference, and have some say in decisions. A short personal thank-you, sharing results ('Our ajo helped 6 members restock this year'), and asking for ideas rather than only giving orders all draw on emotional intelligence.
Match tasks to people's strengths and interests, and ask before assigning.
Notice when someone is overloaded and offer to share their task.
Celebrate milestones together, even with something small like a shared meal.
When someone steps back, ask privately and kindly what has changed, instead of complaining about them in the group.

Remember that your own wellbeing matters as a leader. Leaders who are exhausted find it much harder to stay patient. Share responsibilities, train a deputy, and take breaks so that you can lead well for the long term.

What EI is
Emotional intelligence in plain words
Notice emotions in yourself and others
Understand what they are telling you
Use that to guide what you say and do
A skill you can learn, like sewing
Emotional intelligence, often called EI or EQ, is the ability to notice emotions in yourself and in other people.
It means understanding what those feelings are telling you, and using that to guide what you say and do.
It is not about never getting angry. It is about handling feelings so they help you instead of controlling you.
And it is a skill. Like learning to drive or to sew, it improves with practice.
Worked example
Ngozi's hard morning, with EI
Perceive: my jaw is tight, my voice is rising
Understand: three things went wrong at once
Manage: three slow breaths, calm words
Use: the urgency pushes her to find a backup
For example, Ngozi runs a provisions shop in Onitsha. One morning the generator will not start, the children are late, and a supplier says her goods will come two days late.
Without EI, she shouts at her son and snaps at the supplier.
With EI, she first perceives. She notices her jaw is tight and her voice is rising.
She understands. She tells herself, I am stressed because three things went wrong at once, not because my son is bad.
She manages. She takes three slow breaths, asks her son to help his sisters, and calmly asks the supplier for a firm new date by 12 noon.
And she uses the feeling. The push of urgency gets her to call a second supplier as a backup. Same problems, but her relationships are protected.
Red: high energy, unpleasant. Angry, anxious
Yellow: high energy, pleasant. Excited, proud
Blue: low energy, unpleasant. Sad, lonely
Green: low energy, pleasant. Calm, grateful
If you cannot name what you feel, you cannot manage it. Putting a feeling into words helps calm it. Some call this name it to tame it.
The Mood Meter asks two questions. How much energy do I have? And how pleasant does this feel?
Red is high energy and unpleasant: angry, anxious, frustrated.
Yellow is high energy and pleasant: excited, hopeful, proud.
Blue is low energy and unpleasant: sad, tired, lonely.
Green is low energy and pleasant: calm, content, grateful.
No zone is bad. For example, Aisha, a teacher, said she was just tired. Looking closer, she found the exact words: humiliated and discouraged. Now she knew what she needed.
An urge is not an order. Widen the gap, then choose.
Emotions follow a chain. Something happens, and you add a thought about what it means.
For example, Funmi posts photos of her new tailoring shop on the family WhatsApp group. Two hours later, only her aunt has replied. She thinks, nobody supports me.
She feels hurt, and her body wants to act. The urge is to leave the group.
But an urge is not an order. She checks the evidence. It is a weekday afternoon, and most cousins are at work.
She stays in the group and sends the photos to two cousins directly. By evening she has 9 replies and one cousin has booked a fitting.
Check your thoughts
Fuel thoughts, and three questions
Fuel thoughts
She thinks I am a failure
He never helps
My business is finished
I am useless
Ask yourself
What is the evidence?
What would I tell a friend?
Some thoughts pour fuel on the fire. Mind-reading, always and never, imagining the worst, and calling yourself names.
When you notice one, ask three questions. What is the evidence? What else could explain this? What would I tell a friend who thought this?
This is not pretending everything is fine. If someone really treats you badly, see it clearly and respond wisely.
Know your triggers
Blessing's trigger log
Log every strong reaction for a week
6 of 11 came before 10am
5 of those 6: she was hungry
Plan: eat first, a sign for credit
Next week: 5 reactions, not 11
HALT: am I Hungry, Angry, Lonely or Tired?
A trigger is anything that sets off a reaction bigger than the situation deserves. For example, Blessing sells foodstuff in Port Harcourt. She logs every strong reaction for one week.
6 of her 11 reactions happened before 10am, and 5 of those 6 were marked hungry.
That is the HALT check. Am I hungry, angry, lonely or tired? Any of these makes small problems feel bigger.
So she eats something before leaving home, and writes a clear sign for credit requests.
The next week she logs 5 strong reactions instead of 11.

Remember

Find your zone, then the exact feeling word
Situation, thought, feeling, urge, action
Use HALT and a trigger log

Worked example
STOP: Chioma gets the school fees call
Stop: phone face down, no dialling
Take a breath: one minute of slow breathing
Observe: I am scared and embarrassed
Proceed: call the bursar, then her husband
A reaction is automatic. A response is chosen.
A reaction is fast and automatic: a shout, a slammed door. A response is chosen.
For example, Chioma, a civil servant in Enugu, gets a call at work. Her son's fees are overdue. Her face goes hot and she wants to call her husband and shout.
She uses STOP. Stop: she puts the phone face down and does not dial.
Take a breath: about one minute of slow breathing at her desk.
Observe: I am scared and embarrassed, and I am telling myself he forgot on purpose.
Proceed: she calls the bursar and arranges to pay half today and the rest within two weeks. Then she calls her husband calmly to plan together.
Calm your body in one minute
Breathe in through your nose for 4
Hold gently for 4
Breathe out through your mouth for 4
Hold empty for 4, and repeat 4 times
Practise when calm, so your body knows what to do under stress.
Here is box breathing. Breathe in slowly through your nose for a count of 4.
Hold your breath gently for 4.
Breathe out slowly through your mouth for 4.
Hold empty for 4, and repeat 4 times. If holding feels uncomfortable, skip the holds and just make the out-breath longer. A long out-breath slows the heart.
Practise for two minutes each morning when you are calm. Then the tool is ready when stress hits.
Catch anger low on the ladder
1 to 3, annoyed: name it, speak early
4 to 6, frustrated: STOP, lower your voice
7 to 8, angry: take a time-out now
9 to 10, rage: leave safely, talk later
Anger is a normal signal that something feels unfair. The problem is what we do with it. Anger climbs in steps.
At 1 to 3 you are annoyed. Name it, breathe, and speak early and calmly.
At 4 to 6 your jaw is tight and your voice rises. Use STOP and lower your voice on purpose.
At 7 to 8 your face is hot and your fists are clenched. Take a time-out. Say, I need 20 minutes, let us talk again at 8pm. Then come back as agreed.
At 9 to 10, leave the room safely and talk only when calm.
Then use an I statement. I feel worried when the shop is left unlocked, because we could lose our stock.
Handling stress
Sort what you can control
For example, Zainab, a hairdresser in Abuja, has rent due, two clients who have not paid, and a sick mother. She cannot sleep.
She writes 8 worries on paper. 4 she can act on, so she gives each one a time: call the clients at 9am, the landlord at 11am.
The other 4 she cannot control. For those she breathes slowly at night and says, I have done what I can today.
By Thursday one client has paid and the landlord gives her 5 extra days.
Your safety first
When to get help straight away
Being hit, threatened or controlled is not an anger problem. Go somewhere safe and get help.
Low most days for over two weeks, or cannot eat, sleep or care for yourself: see a doctor.
Thoughts of harming yourself? Go to the nearest hospital or tell someone close at once.

Some things breathing cannot fix. If you or someone at home is being hit, threatened or controlled, your safety comes first. Go to a safe place, and contact trusted family, the police or an organisation that supports women.

Sadness after a loss is normal, and grief moves back and forth. But if low mood lasts most days for more than two weeks, or you cannot eat, sleep or care for your children, see a doctor or counsellor.
If you have any thoughts of harming yourself, go to the nearest hospital emergency unit or tell someone close to you immediately.
Bounce back
Amaka reframes a rejected loan
Personal: not my failing, a fixable reason
Pervasive: one area, the rest is good
Permanent: 6 months of records, then reapply
Connection: join an ajo as a second route
Resilience is a set of skills anyone can learn. How you explain a setback affects how fast you recover.
For example, Amaka is turned down for a business loan. She thinks, I am not good at business, nothing works for me, I will never grow.
Personal: she asks why. She had no 6-month bank statement showing regular sales. That is fixable.
Pervasive: her customers are happy and her sister supports her.
Permanent: if she puts all her sales through her account for 6 months, she can reapply.
And she joins a weekly ajo with 9 other traders. A setback became a plan with two routes.
Key points
Remember
STOP gives you a gap to choose
Box breathing: 4 in, hold, 4 out, hold
Take a time-out at anger level 7 or above
Act on what you control; accept the rest
Safety first; get help when it is serious
To remember. STOP gives you a gap. Box breathing calms the body. Take a time-out early, and come back. Act on what you control. And when it is serious, put your safety first and get help.

What empathy is
Understanding how someone thinks and sees the situation.
Feeling something of what they feel.
Understanding, feeling, and being moved to help, while staying steady.
Empathy is understanding and sharing another person's feelings and point of view. It does not mean agreeing with everything they do.
Cognitive empathy is understanding how someone thinks. She is worried her boss will think she is lazy.
Emotional empathy is feeling something of what they feel. Too little can seem cold. Too much, with no boundaries, can leave you drained.
Compassionate empathy balances the two. You care, and you stay steady enough to help.
Connect, don't distance
At least you still have...
That sounds really hard
Sympathy looks down from a distance. Oh, poor you. It often reaches for a silver lining that starts with at least.
Empathy climbs down beside the person. That sounds really hard, and you are not alone.
Worked example
Joy listens to Halima
Give full attention
Listen for facts and feelings
Reflect back what you heard
Check you understood
Ask before advising
For example, Halima tells her friend Joy that her company has laid off 20 staff, including her.
An unhelpful reply would be, at least you got a package, don't worry.
Instead, Joy steps away from the TV and gives full attention. She listens for the facts and the feelings.
She reflects back. Eight years there, and they told you by email. You must be shocked, and worried about the children's fees.
Halima says yes, and embarrassed. I don't know how to tell my mother.
Joy asks, do you want to think through what to say, or do you just need to vent tonight?
Halima feels understood. The next day they draft her CV together.
Reading people
Look at face, voice and body
Look for a cluster of cues

Much of what people feel is shown, not said. For example, Ronke runs a catering business. Her assistant Tolu usually jokes while cooking. For three days Tolu has been quiet, avoiding eye contact and leaving exactly on time.
That is a cluster of cues, and a change from her normal.
Culture matters too. In many Nigerian families, a younger person avoids eye contact with an elder out of respect, not dishonesty.
So Ronke does not guess that Tolu is lazy. She asks privately. You have seemed quieter this week. Is everything okay? No pressure.
Tolu's mother is in hospital. Ronke lets her leave early for two weeks, and Tolu's loyalty grows.
Ijeoma raises a problem kindly
Start with I feel
How a hard conversation starts usually decides how it ends.
Criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling damage relationships. Each has an antidote.
For example, Ijeoma and her sister Nneka run a cosmetics stall in Aba. Nneka arrives late most days. The old way was, you are so unserious, said in front of customers.
The new way, in private: I feel stressed when I open alone, because the morning rush is our busiest hour. Could you be here by 8am, or can we agree which days you open?
Nneka explains she has been taking their mother to the clinic. Ijeoma says, I didn't know, I'm sorry I assumed. They agree a rota, and the problem is solved in ten minutes.
Emotion coaching
Bukola coaches Dami at the party
Notice the emotion early
Help name the feeling
Set limits, solve the problem
All feelings are allowed. Not all behaviour is.
For example, Bukola's 6-year-old daughter Dami screams and throws her plate at a birthday, because she did not get the piece with the candle. Bukola saw her face crumple first, and kneels down.
Instead of shouting, she takes Dami's hand and moves a few steps from the crowd.
She validates. You really wanted the piece with the candle. That is disappointing.
She helps name it. Are you feeling disappointed, and a bit jealous? Dami nods.
Then the limit. It is okay to feel disappointed. Throwing plates is not okay. Let us pick it up together. Next time, what can you do? Dami says, tell you. She calms in about 3 minutes.
Key points
Remember
Empathy connects; sympathy keeps a distance
Reflect, check, then ask before advising
Read clusters of cues, then ask gently
Start hard talks gently, in private
Never use fear or harsh punishment
To remember. Listen and reflect before you advise. Read clusters of cues and check gently. Start hard talks gently.

With children, use positive, non-violent discipline. If you feel close to losing control, put the child somewhere safe, step away and call someone you trust. And if someone repeatedly threatens or harms you, seek support. That is not a communication problem.

Worked example
LAST: Patience calms an angry customer
Listen: one bottle arrived broken
Apologise: I am sorry this happened
Solve: a free replacement tomorrow
Thank: thank you for telling me quickly
Calm the feeling first. Then solving the problem is easier.
For example, Patience sells hair products on Instagram from Benin City. A customer's order of 3 bottles of hair oil arrives with one broken, and she sends a voice note calling Patience a scammer.
Patience feels insulted. She uses STOP and waits 10 minutes before replying.
Listen. I hear you. You paid for 3 bottles and one arrived broken. That is very disappointing.
Apologise. I am sorry this happened. She does not argue about the word scammer.
Solve. Please send a photo. I will send a replacement with my rider tomorrow at no cost, and pack in bubble wrap from now on.
Thank. Thank you for letting me know quickly.
The customer leaves a positive review and orders again the next month.
Giving feedback
The SBI model: situation, behaviour, impact
You are careless with customers
Well done
Situation: Tuesday afternoon
Behaviour: kept looking at the phone
Impact: she left without buying
Then ask: what happened?
Feedback like you are careless judges the person. Even well done is too vague to learn from.

SBI keeps it fair. Say the situation: at the shop on Tuesday afternoon. The behaviour: when the woman asked about prices, you kept looking at your phone. The impact: she left without buying. Then ask for their view.
When you receive criticism, breathe, listen to the end, and ask for an example.
Money safety
Scams play on your emotions
Your account will be blocked.
Double your money in 7 days.
Pay now or lose the offer.
Strong feelings push poor money decisions. Many scams are built to make you feel fear. Your account will be blocked.
Or greed. Double your money in 7 days.
Or urgency. Pay now or lose the offer.

A rush of emotion around money is your signal to slow down. Never share your BVN, card PIN or OTP, and check with your bank on its official number. For any big decision in the red zone, wait 24 hours.
Marriage and partnership
Adaeze and Tunde agree a money plan
For example, Adaeze and her husband Tunde argue every month about money for his brothers.
Combined monthly income
Into savings first
Fixed family support
Talk first if an extra is above
Naira figures are approximate.
For example, Adaeze and her husband Tunde both work in Lagos. Tunde sends money to his younger brothers, and Adaeze feels the household is left short.
On a calm Saturday she starts gently. I feel anxious about our savings when large amounts go out without planning. Can we sit down with the numbers?
Tunde explains his need. As the first son, supporting his brothers matters deeply to him. Adaeze shares hers: security for their own children. They write their combined income, about 650,000 naira.
They put 50,000 naira into savings first, and agree a fixed 80,000 naira a month for family support.
Any extra request above 20,000 naira, they discuss together first. The difference in values remains, but the monthly fight stops.
Community leadership
Folake mediates a cooperative quarrel
Move it out of the group chat
Meet privately and set rules
Each tells her side; reflect feelings
Find the shared goal
Agree clear, recorded next steps
Criticise actions, never a person's family or character.

For example, Folake chairs a women's thrift cooperative in Ilorin. Two members quarrel in the WhatsApp group about missed contributions. Folake posts: let us not discuss this here. I will meet you both on Saturday.
At the meeting she sets rules. One person speaks at a time, no insults.
Each tells her side, and Folake reflects their feelings. Kafayat feels it is unfair. Mama Sade is embarrassed, because flooding closed her shop for a month.
Both want the cooperative to survive and stay trusted.
Mama Sade agrees to repay in four weekly instalments, recorded by the treasurer, and the group writes a clear rule for missed payments.
